name: Foam roller

lead: A foam roller is a cylinder of dense foam, typically 15 to 90 cm long, on which a person rolls their body weight against muscle groups. It is used for self-massage before or after training.
For posture it is also used lengthwise or crosswise under the upper back for thoracic extension, a popular drill for desk workers.

paras: Pressure on the tissue is thought to reduce perceived stiffness through neural and sensory effects rather than by breaking up fascia. A multilevel meta-analysis of 26 trials found foam rolling increases joint range of motion acutely, and a 2022 meta-analysis found no significant difference from stretching immediately afterward or later. Training effects over weeks on range of motion are small.

Aggressive rolling can cause bruising and soreness, and rolling over the lower back, joints or neck is discouraged. Effects are short-lived, and no evidence shows that rolling permanently corrects posture or releases knots; benefits for range of motion and perceived soreness are reported as modest.

lead: A foam roller is a cylinder of dense foam, commonly 30 to 90 cm long and 12 to 15 cm in diameter, on which a person rolls their body weight over muscle groups as a form of self-massage, often called self-myofascial release.[1] It is used before or after training, and in posture-oriented routines it is also placed under the upper back for thoracic extension exercises, a drill popular among people who sit for long periods.

A sizeable research literature examines foam rolling. Meta-analyses report that rolling increases joint range of motion acutely, with effects on performance that are small, and that its effect on range of motion is comparable to stretching.[2][3][4][5] Studies of training effects over weeks report small changes in range of motion.[4] Evidence on soreness and recovery is mixed, and no trial cited in this article tests whether thoracic-extension rolling produces lasting changes in resting posture.
infobox: Smooth, textured or grid surfaces; vibrating rollers; roller sticks
Associated with the Feldenkrais Method; adapted for self-massage in the late 1980s

paras: Rollers are made from foam (commonly EVA or similar elastomers) in varying densities. Surfaces may be smooth or have ridges and grids intended to deliver a more focused pressure. A Grokipedia article lists typical dimensions of 12 to 36 inches in length and 5 to 6 inches in diameter.[1] Related tools include roller sticks and massage balls, and in recent years vibrating foam rollers.[6]
A 2008 laboratory study compared the pressure exerted on soft tissue by two types of myofascial rollers,[7] reflecting a long-standing interest in how roller design relates to tissue loading.

A Grokipedia account traces the foam roller to the Feldenkrais Method, a somatic-education approach founded by Moshe Feldenkrais, who is reported to have used foam rollers as supports in movement lessons. The same article says the physical therapist Sean Gallagher, who trained as a Feldenkrais practitioner, adapted rollers for clinical self-massage in 1987, and that Mike Clark helped bring them into athletic training in the 1990s.[1] The article states that the American College of Sports Medicine ranked foam rolling the fourteenth global fitness trend of 2019.[1] These details come from an AI-generated source and the dates in it are not entirely consistent, so they are given as that source's account.

Rolling applies sustained pressure, generated by body weight, to the soft tissue. The older explanation, that rolling breaks up fascial adhesions or knots, has been questioned. The encyclopedia summary describes limited evidence for mechanical changes in tissue stiffness and favours explanations based on the nervous system, such as increased stretch tolerance and pain modulation through mechanoreceptor input (gate-control theory), plus possible parasympathetic effects.[1] It adds that the precise mechanisms are still under investigation.[1]

A systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis in Sports Medicine in 2020 pooled trials of acute foam rolling and reported increases in joint range of motion in healthy adults.[2] A 2022 meta-analysis of training effects over weeks found small improvements in range of motion.[4] A 2022 trial in the European Journal of Applied Physiology compared a single bout of stretching with foam rolling in healthy adults.[3] A 2013 laboratory study of 11 active men reported that an acute bout of self-myofascial release increased knee range of motion without a subsequent decrease in muscle activation or force.[8] Randomised trials have also compared foam rolling with proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation stretching for hamstring flexibility in amateur athletes[9] and examined effects on muscle flexibility in recreational long-distance runners.[10]

A 2019 meta-analysis of 21 studies in Frontiers in Physiology reported that rolling before exercise produced a small improvement in sprint performance (about 0.7 per cent, g = 0.28), among other findings, and also covered rolling used after exercise as a recovery strategy.[11] A 2015 systematic review in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy appraised foam rolls and roller massagers for range of motion, post-exercise muscle recovery and performance.[5] A 2014 randomised study of 20 trained men tested foam rolling as a recovery tool after an intense bout of exercise, with soreness, range of motion and vertical jump among its outcomes.[12] A 2023 meta-analysis of five studies with 151 participants found no significant between-group difference between foam roller or stick massage and non-intervention after muscle-damaging exercise on the markers analysed, with studies at moderate to high risk of bias.[13]
A 2022 meta-analysis of vibrating foam rollers, including 9 studies, found no significant effect on jump performance (SMD 0.14).[6]

Thoracic extension rolling is a widely shared routine in posture communities. The trials above mostly examine limb muscles and athletic outcomes. A 2017 randomised trial examined whether foam-roller exercises have a short-term effect on the thoracolumbar fascia,[14] and a 2019 randomised trial examined the training effects of foam rolling on core strength endurance, balance, performance and range of motion.[15] No study cited here shows that using a roller under the upper back changes resting spinal alignment over the long term.

The encyclopedia summary describes foam rolling as generally safe but advises avoiding direct pressure on bones, joints and injured areas, and consulting a health-care provider in conditions such as acute tears, pregnancy or chronic conditions.[1] Rolling firmly can leave bruising or soreness. Guidance from clinicians commonly cautions against rolling over the lower back and neck, where the spine is not shielded by large muscle masses.

In posture and mobility sections of appearance communities, the roller is typically described as a way to open a rounded upper back and loosen tight areas before exercises that target the muscles between and below the shoulder blades. Proponents describe a feeling of increased upright posture and loosened muscles after a session. Research summarised above supports short-term increases in range of motion, and the effects that last are described as small.

A large number of controlled studies exist, mostly in healthy active adults and athletes. Meta-analyses report acute increases in joint range of motion,[2] small training effects on range of motion over weeks,[4] small pre-exercise effects on sprint performance and flexibility,[11] no significant effect of vibration rollers on jump performance[6] and no significant difference from non-intervention for soreness markers after muscle-damaging exercise in a small meta-analysis with high risk of bias.[13] Individual randomised trials have compared rolling with stretching[3][9][10] and examined thoracolumbar fascia and core outcomes.[14][15] A 2023 systematic review of myofascial release strategies in athletes included both instrument-assisted mobilisation and foam rolling, reporting that foam rolling was relevant for counter-movement jump performance.[16] Plantar-fasciitis reviews also include foam roller stretching among physiotherapy interventions.[17]

timeline.event: Physical therapist Sean Gallagher is reported to have adapted foam rollers for clinical self-massage.[1]
A laboratory study reports increased range of motion after self-myofascial release without a subsequent decrease in activation or force.[8]
Meta-analysis of foam rolling on performance and recovery is published; the American College of Sports Medicine ranks foam rolling a top fitness trend, per Grokipedia.[1][11]
Multilevel meta-analysis reports acute range-of-motion increases from foam rolling.[2]
Meta-analyses examine foam-rolling training effects and vibrating rollers.[4][6]
